title: The Letter at the Bell
logline: When old Mr Hale dies without a will that anyone can find, the quiet woman who reads everyone else's letters before they do discovers his was never lost at all, only never opened.
promise: A missing will is found honestly, a fortune hunter is exposed by his own haste, and the person quietly thanked for a kindness turns out not to be the one who did it.
setting: Amberlight and the neighbouring farm at Hale's Bottom, autumn 1816

cast.name: Miss Judith Vane
cast.station: keeps house for her brother, the apothecary; no fortune of her own
cast.want: to see the true will found before Constance Wray is married out of her own inheritance
cast.appearance: Fair, freckled, of middling height, with reddish hair she cannot keep pinned and a habit of looking directly at whoever is speaking.
cast.dress: Sprigged muslin in summer, a grey wool pelisse in winter, both mended with more thrift than skill.
cast.voice_note: quiet, precise, waits a beat before answering

cast.name: Mr Edward Sorrel
cast.station: clerk to a Winchester firm of solicitors, sent to settle the Hale estate; salary modest but a partnership expected
cast.want: to close the estate correctly, whatever it costs him with the family that pays his firm
cast.appearance: tall, sandy-haired, ink permanently at the side of one finger, spectacles he forgets he is wearing
cast.dress: a serviceable brown coat, always slightly travel-creased
cast.voice_note: formal at first meeting, dryly funny once he trusts you

cast.name: Mr Peter Hale
cast.station: nephew of the late Josiah Hale; gentleman of no settled income and considerable debt
cast.want: to secure Hale's Bottom farm by marriage or by default before any will can surface
cast.appearance: handsome in an obvious way, well-fed, fair curls kept a little too fashionably long
cast.dress: a blue coat cut better than his circumstances warrant
cast.voice_note: charming, quick to laugh, quicker to change the subject

cast.name: Miss Constance Wray
cast.station: ward and niece by marriage to the late Josiah Hale; raised in his house, no independent fortune
cast.want: to keep the farm and the life she has always known without being married for it
cast.appearance: small and fair, with a stillness that some mistake for meekness
cast.voice_note: soft-spoken, says exactly what she means and no more

cast.name: Mrs Honoria Pike
cast.station: widow of a naval surgeon; three hundred a year and a house on the green
cast.want: to know everything before anyone else does
cast.appearance: Short and broad, with grey hair pinned severely under a lace cap, and small quick eyes set in a round weathered face.
cast.dress: Black bombazine with a plain white fichu, ten years out of fashion and immaculately kept.
cast.voice_note: brisk, talks over people cheerfully, certain of things she has half-heard

cast.name: Mr Silas Rowe
cast.station: curate of Amberlight; eighty a year and no expectations
cast.want: to have done his duty by a dying parishioner, once he can remember exactly what that duty was
cast.appearance: Tall and thin, dark hair worn slightly too long, with the stoop of a man used to low doorways and a face that gives away more than he intends.
cast.dress: Worn black coat, carefully brushed, and linen that has been turned at the cuffs.
cast.voice_note: earnest, apologetic, loses the thread mid-sentence

cast.name: Mrs Eliza Thorne
cast.station: former housekeeper to Josiah Hale, now living alone on a small annuity
cast.want: to be believed, since no one has troubled to ask her anything until now
cast.appearance: broad, red-knuckled hands, grey hair scraped back, a face used to being overlooked
cast.dress: a faded print gown and a housekeeper's apron kept from long habit
cast.voice_note: flat, guarded, warms slowly once taken seriously

chapters.title: The Farm Without a Will
beats: Old Mr Josiah Hale of Hale's Bottom farm dies after a short illness, attended in his last days by Judith Vane's brother the apothecary.
Mrs Pike declares over tea that no will has been found, and that the farm, worth some hundred and fifty a year, must therefore pass to the nephew, Mr Peter Hale.
Constance Wray, Hale's grieving ward of four-and-twenty, is seen at church in mourning black, uncertain whether she will keep her home past Michaelmas.
Peter Hale is already telling neighbours he means to 'keep the farm in the family,' with a warm look toward Constance that Judith finds too quick for grief.

A clerk from the Winchester solicitors, Mr Edward Sorrel, arrives at the Bell to settle the estate and admits, pressed by Mrs Pike, that Hale told his lawyers years ago he had left everything in order — and that no such document can be found.

chapters.title: A Man in a Hurry
beats: Judith meets Sorrel at the circulating library, both there ostensibly for other business, and compares what each has heard.
Sorrel confirms that under the law, if no will is found, the farm goes to Peter as next of kin, and that he has one fortnight before he must report the estate settled.
Judith recalls her brother mentioning that old Hale, in his last week, spoke of a letter he meant to send to his solicitor and asked after the coach days.
Peter Hale, overhearing part of this in the shop, laughs it off as an old man's confusion and steers the conversation to his own plans for the farm.
Judith decides to ask her brother exactly what Hale said, and finds, when she does, that Hale named no solicitor at all but only said the letter was 'given already.'

chapters.title: The Housekeeper's Drawer
beats: Judith and Sorrel call on Mrs Thorne, Hale's former housekeeper, now living alone at the edge of the parish.
Mrs Thorne recalls a letter arriving for her, oddly, in the week before Hale's death, sealed and heavy, which she set aside unread, thinking it none of her business.
She goes to the kitchen drawer to produce it and finds the drawer disturbed, the letter gone.
She admits Peter Hale called on her only three days past, alone, on some pretext of settling her annuity, and was left waiting in that very kitchen.
Sorrel points out that a stolen letter proves nothing was destroyed that mattered, only that someone believed it did — which means the true document may exist elsewhere still.

chapters.title: A Proposal in Church
beats: Peter Hale, before the fortnight is out, proposes to Constance publicly after Sunday service, framing it as securing her future and the farm together.
Constance, cornered by the audience of the whole parish, asks only for time to consider, which Peter grants with visible impatience.
Mrs Pike is seen delivering a basket to Constance's door and is thanked warmly for her continued kindness, which she accepts without correcting anyone.
Judith notices the basket contains more than charity usually allows — good linen, coin wrapped in paper — and wonders where a widow of three hundred a year finds such generosity twice a month.
Mr Rowe, asked in passing whether Hale left anything with him before he died, goes pale and says he believes there may have been 'something in the vestry papers' he never got round to sorting.

chapters.title: What the Curate Forgot
beats: Judith and Sorrel search the vestry with Rowe, who apologises repeatedly for the state of his correspondence.
Among unanswered parish letters they find a sealed envelope addressed not to any solicitor but to Mrs Thorne, in Hale's own hand.

Rowe remembers now: Hale came to him privately, distrusting the post after a parcel once went astray, and asked him to hold the letter until Mrs Thorne could be sent for it — then Rowe forgot entirely.
With Mrs Thorne and Constance both fetched as witnesses, Sorrel opens the seal.
The letter is Hale's true will, naming Constance sole heir of Hale's Bottom, and stating plainly that Peter's portion was already given him years before, in full, as settlement of his gambling debts.

chapters.title: The Nephew's Portion
beats: Word of the will spreads within the hour, and Peter Hale arrives at the Bell demanding to see it himself.
Sorrel reads aloud the passage naming the sum Hale paid to clear Peter's debts, which matches almost exactly the sum Peter has always claimed he raised 'on his own credit.'
Peter, cornered, insists the letter is a forgery, got up by Judith and the clerk to rob him of what is his.

It emerges that the basket money Mrs Pike has been delivering to Constance these past weeks was in fact never hers to give — she was only asked, by Rowe, to pass along sums Hale had left for that purpose before his death, and never thought to say so.
Mrs Pike, mortified at being thanked for someone else's kindness these many weeks, declares she will get to the bottom of this before nightfall — and marches straight for Mr Rowe.

chapters.title: The Handwriting
beats: Peter demands proof the will is genuinely Hale's hand and not some clerk's imitation.
Judith's brother produces old prescription notes in his shop bearing Hale's signature from years back, matched letter for letter against the will by Sorrel.
Mrs Thorne confirms the seal as Hale's own, the one he always used, kept in a particular drawer she alone dusted.
Rowe, gaining courage, states plainly before the assembled parish that Hale gave him the letter with his own hands and his own instructions, which Rowe is ashamed only to have forgotten so long.
Peter, seeing the room turn against him, tells Constance sharply that she was always meant to marry him regardless, and Constance answers, quietly and for everyone to hear, that she is not.

chapters.title: What Was Settled
beats: Peter Hale leaves Amberlight within the week, his debts and his disappointment both now common knowledge.
Constance takes possession of Hale's Bottom and keeps Mrs Thorne on as housekeeper, this time properly paid.

Constance tries to thank Mrs Pike once more for her kindness, and Mrs Pike, laughing at herself now, insists the thanks belong to a dead man and a forgetful curate, not to her — though she allows she delivered the baskets very well.

Sorrel, his business concluded, calls on Judith to say his firm will want a resident agent to oversee such small estates hereabouts, and asks, with more hesitation than his profession usually allows, whether Amberlight might suit him permanently.
Judith says it might suit them both, and the parish settles back into its usual business of watching the coach come in on Tuesdays and Fridays, with one fewer thing left unresolved.
